title: What Is the Sound of One Hand Clapping?
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos, a first-grade reading interventionist, recounts an email exchange with a whole-language professor that never became a real conversation. She sets out the points she raised, including quotations from Stanovich, Adams, Ehri, Shanahan and others against three-cueing and for decoding as the on-ramp to word recognition, and notes that each drew no response. Her argument is that the reading wars persist partly because the two camps do not engage with each other's evidence, and that Max Planck's line about science advancing one funeral at a time is too slow for children who are instructional casualties. She leans on Steve Dykstra's point that teachers must have right reasons they can explain to colleagues and must know where the science ends and judgment begins. The piece closes by contrasting the silence of her exchange with Tim Odegard's more open treatment of screening dilemmas, and by treating each child's reading failure as a shared responsibility. It is part rebuttal file and part lament, but the research citations on three-cueing, decoding and orthographic mapping give it substance.
points: Janetos catalogues researchers (Stanovich, Adams, Ehri, Shanahan, Vaughn and Clemens, Goldenberg) who reject three-cueing, and records that her interlocutor answered none of them.
Her practical model is explicit teaching of grapheme-phoneme connections with flexible pronunciations, with decoding treated as the on-ramp to orthographic mapping and word recognition.
Dykstra's standard that teachers need explainable reasons rather than certainty gives a workable test for instructional decisions when evidence is incomplete.
She argues that professional discourse itself fails when positions are asserted rather than defended with cited evidence, and that this delay is paid for by struggling readers.
quotes: Unfortunately, there was no dialogue or discussion in this exchange—just a series of emphatic declarations from the professor about how the brain is a meaning-making machine with implications for instruction based on cognitive science studies generally related to memory rather than specifically related to reading acquisition. These declarations were usually followed by either silence or deflection after I responded to the points made.

Here’s German physicist Max Planck’s oft-quoted statement about science: A new scientific truth does not triumph by convincing opponents and making them see the light, but rather because its opponents eventually die, and a new generation grows up that is familiar with it.
Agreed! But if we share articles without discussing them, that's not a conversation--it's a swap meet!
This was never a conversation. Not once! It was a tribute to the prison warden in the Paul Newman film Cool Hand Luke with the oft-quoted line: What we’ve got here is failure to communicate.
We are not required to be right; we are required to have ‘right’ reasons that we can explain to other professionals . . . Know where the science ends and your best judgment begins.

The point is that if we can’t explain our reasons for our instructional choices to our fellow professionals, challenge the rightness of each other’s reasons, and discuss them freely and frankly, our profession won’t advance faster (to paraphrase Max Planck) than one funeral at a time—which is simply too slow to impact those students who are instructional casualties.

But the reality is that it’s not me but our students who are being played because they’re the ones who are subjected to the imprisonment of outdated, outlandish reading methods that are tethered to tenuous ideas about reading acquisition. Despite the consensus among researchers (and confirmed by my experiences working with hundreds of students) that we need to facilitate orthographic mapping to make words stick, there continue to be practices that prevent this glue factory from setting up shop in our schools and becoming a fully functioning part of classroom instruction.
